Warm-up

  1. What picture do you see first when you hear the word Australia?

  2. Have you ever met anyone who lived in or visited Australia?

  3. Do you prefer formal talk or free talk with strangers in a shop?

Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: Australian culture for adult learners begins with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, often called First Nations peoples. These are among the oldest continuing cultures on Earth, with deep time continuity on this land. One key word is Country. In the First Nations sense, Country is a living land relationship. It is not only a place on a map. It links people with land and with a wider living world. This careful idea helps explain why First Nations cultures remain central to Australian life today.

Part 2: Convicts, settlers, and the fair go

Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: In 1788 the First Fleet arrived. This was a group of British ships that came to Sydney in New South Wales with convicts and officials. British colonisation, convict transportation, and settler society followed from that beginning. A strong idea in Australian talk is the fair go. It means people should get a fair chance. Next to it sits tall poppy syndrome, a common pattern of cutting down people who seem too proud or above others. These are patterns in talk, not a perfect picture of every person. Still, they help explain why equal treatment matters in much Australian talk.

Typing practice

Text to type: Australia is a large place, and the bush is part of national talk about land far from easy city comfort. Distance between places shaped practical habits and outdoor life. In coastal cities, beach time, park time, and sport are easy to notice. Weekend outdoor plans are common in daily conversation. The bush and the coast together help explain why outdoor life and sport sit near the centre of Australian culture.

Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: Post-war immigration changed Australian city life. The White Australia policy era ended, and multicultural centres grew. Sydney and Melbourne are clear examples. In daily city life, visitors can notice many languages and foods. Local streets and festivals show family stories from many countries. Modern Australian city culture is hard to understand without immigration waves and multicultural life.

Part 5: Mateship, friendly manners, and direct talk

Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: Mateship is a famous Australian idea. It means loyal friendship and support between equals. It is linked to informal manners and helping one another. The friendly word mate often appears in everyday talk. Australian manners can feel free to visitors. People may use first names quickly and speak in a direct way. Direct talk is not always rude talk. It often means saying the main point without long ceremony. Mateship sits beside fair go ideas: help people, stay equal, and keep talk open.

Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: Anzac Day is on 25 April. It remembers the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, or ANZAC, at Gallipoli in 1915, and later service. Dawn services are part of that shared national memory. Visitors also notice brighter public signs: famous city places, beach culture, and sport stories. These are not the whole of Australian life, but they give people common pictures. Under them sit First Nations Country, the First Fleet and fair go talk, distance and outdoor life, immigration, and mateship.

1. What is Anzac Day, and why do visitors notice it?

Sample answer

Anzac Day is 25 April, when Australia remembers ANZAC service from Gallipoli in 1915 and later service, often with dawn services, so visitors notice it as shared national memory.

What national day in your country feels serious and shared for you?
